title: Safe, repeatable rejuvenation of an aged human body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that restores youthful function broadly across an aged human body, can be repeated safely, and preserves cognition and personal identity. Its defining outcome would be recovery of established functional decline across tissues and organs. Changes in molecular measurements would help explain or track that recovery, but would not by themselves establish rejuvenation. This is the target capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement.

Partial cellular reprogramming is one possible route. The supplied 2020 study investigated resetting age-associated epigenetic features while retaining specialized cell identity, and reported localized functional recovery using OSK expression in mice. That provides a technical basis for investigating repair through altered cell states, while leaving the much broader challenge of safe, repeatable human rejuvenation unresolved by these experiments.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if treatment could durably restore function across several aged human organs while preserving brain function and identity, substantial established age-related decline would become repairable in treated people. The direct consequence would be recovery of measured abilities and physiological function. The mouse vision findings support the narrower premise that some age-associated functional loss can respond to a reprogramming intervention; they do not establish that this can be extended safely across human organs.

Conditional downstream possibilities include longer periods of independence, reduced disability and less need for care, provided functional recovery translates into durable everyday benefit. These are implications of the proposed capability rather than demonstrated outcomes. Benefits could differ substantially between organs, diseases and individuals, so successful treatment of one form of decline would not establish comprehensive reversal of aging.

An analogy to resetting a biological clock has important limits. Resetting an age-associated molecular measurement does not establish that all relevant tissue damage has been repaired, that lost cells have been replaced, or that cancer risk has been controlled. Even successful, repeatable functional rejuvenation would not establish indefinite lifespan extension; effects on survival and remaining causes of illness and death would require separate evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central challenge is to turn localized recovery into broad, coordinated restoration of function with an acceptable safety profile. Reprogramming must alter age-associated cell states without erasing the specialized identities that allow tissues to function. The supplied paper explicitly addresses this distinction and discusses teratomas and fatal dysplasia associated with continuous OSKM expression. Those concerns motivate careful control of reprogramming, but they should not be treated as measured risks of every OSK regimen or of an unspecified future human treatment.

Engineering synthesis: a body-wide approach would need adequate delivery to relevant tissues, control over the extent and duration of treatment, and evidence that different organs tolerate the intervention while recovering useful function. Repeated administration adds a further requirement: benefit must persist or be recoverable without progressively accumulating harm. The supplied localized functional experiments do not resolve these delivery, coordination or repeat-treatment questions.

Additional proposed assessment targets include mutations, cell loss and extracellular damage. A treatment that changes cell state might leave some of these problems unresolved, but the supplied evidence does not establish their persistence or correction under a systemic human rejuvenation regimen. Immune injury is likewise a safety concern to investigate, rather than a treatment effect characterized here. Establishing which forms of damage an intervention repairs, leaves unchanged or worsens is part of defining its practical limits.

The scientific gap is therefore broader than making molecular age measurements appear younger: it includes demonstrating durable functional recovery, retaining tissue organization and specialized identity, and preserving cognition and personal identity in humans. The historical evidence supplied here cannot establish whether the overall capability remained unavailable in November 2026; it establishes a narrower experimental starting point.

current_state.text: Yuancheng Lu, Benedikt Brommer, Xiao Tian and colleagues reported localized reprogramming results in “Reprogramming to recover youthful epigenetic information and restore vision,” published online in Nature on 2 December 2020, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2975-4. The study reported optic-nerve axon regeneration and improved visual function in a mouse model of induced glaucoma. In the glaucoma experiments, the optomotor response assay indicated restoration of approximately half the visual acuity lost following increased intraocular pressure. This quantitative result concerns a specific mouse model and assay, not recovery of half of all visual function or a human treatment effect.

For age-associated decline, the paper reported restoration of reduced visual acuity and retinal ganglion cell electrical activity in 12-month-old mice following OSK induction. Visual-acuity restoration was not observed in 18-month-old mice; the authors suggested that corneal opacity hindered assessment. That explanation remains the authors’ interpretation: the older-mouse result does not demonstrate restoration, and the assessment limitation prevents a simple conclusion about why restoration was not observed.

The paper also includes systemic mouse safety experiments and human cell-culture experiments. Their inclusion broadens the experimental scope beyond local mouse-eye treatment, but does not turn the localized functional findings into evidence of systemic human rejuvenation. The supplied review verified the paper’s identity and assessed its results text and methods. The retained document contains the main article, methods and references, while referenced extended data and supplementary materials are absent; the review did not require inspection of figure images to support the reported functional findings.

The supplied ClinicalTrials.gov artifact associated with NCT07290244 contains generic interface text rather than substantive study content. Its intervention, phase, design, update date and results therefore cannot be verified from the supplied material. The earlier characterization of it as a phase 1 OSK-delivery study for optic-nerve conditions is not retained as an established fact. This access limitation does not show that the study is nonexistent or that its earlier description is false. Even a confirmed registration alone would establish a registered study, not clinical benefit.

No substantive freshness search record was supplied to establish the state of the field as of 1 November 2026. This account therefore preserves the dated 2020 findings without claiming to be a complete assessment of subsequent research or clinical progress. That limitation does not invalidate the documented mouse results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration of broad functional rejuvenation: randomized, controlled human studies in older adults with measurable decline would show durable, clinically meaningful improvements in independently measured function across several organ systems, including cognition. Outcomes should distinguish recovery of established decline from slower subsequent deterioration. Functional benefit would be necessary; a younger-looking molecular clock alone would be insufficient. These are proposed criteria, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Durable clinically meaningful recovery across several organ systems including cognition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety assessment: studies would prespecify measures of specialized cell-identity preservation, immune injury and other organ-specific harms, together with long-term cancer surveillance. Cognitive measures would assess preservation as well as improvement; preserving personal identity would require an explicit assessment approach rather than an assumption based on bodily recovery. Acceptable risks, follow-up duration and clinically meaningful benefit thresholds remain to be specified.
completion_criteria.label: Safety assessment includes identity preservation and long-term cancer surveillance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration of repeatability: repeated treatment would maintain or renew functional benefit while allowing detection of cumulative toxicity, diminishing effectiveness and delayed harm. Independent replication and consistent results across relevant patient groups would strengthen confidence. Treatment schedules, delivery methods and the populations for which benefits outweigh risks would need clear practical boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated treatment sustains functional benefit with cumulative toxicity assessment

completion_criteria.text: Several improved organ systems would establish broad multi-organ benefit within the tested conditions. A claim of restoration throughout the body would require correspondingly broader evidence, including explicit reporting of tissues, functions and forms of damage that remain uncorrected. Finite studies can establish demonstrated breadth and durability over their observation periods; they cannot prove literal universality, unlimited safe repetition or indefinite survival.
completion_criteria.label: Report demonstrated rejuvenation breadth, durability, and remaining uncorrected damage

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — LON-01, “A predictive causal theory of mammalian aging”: a causal theory could guide the selection and interpretation of rejuvenation interventions. LON-02 concerns demonstrated restoration of function; it would not by itself establish a comprehensive causal theory, and a theory alone would not demonstrate a successful treatment.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-03, “A validated human intervention that greatly slows systemic aging”: slowing further decline and restoring function already lost are distinct outcomes that could coexist in one treatment. Evidence of a slower aging trajectory would not automatically establish rejuvenation, while restored function would not automatically establish a sustained reduction in the rate of aging.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-04, “A fast, validated surrogate for human longevity trials”: a validated surrogate could accelerate evaluation of interventions relevant to LON-02. Its usefulness would depend on what outcomes it predicts. A biomarker shift alone would not satisfy the proposed requirement for demonstrated functional recovery, and prediction of longevity would not automatically establish recovery across organs.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-05, “In-place repair of accumulated molecular damage in old tissues”: direct damage repair could contribute to rejuvenation or complement reprogramming. LON-05 is defined by repair of accumulated damage in tissues, whereas LON-02 is defined by safe, repeatable recovery of aged-body function. Whether a particular reprogramming treatment also repairs particular damage classes requires separate evidence.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-06, “Transfer of exceptional longevity mechanisms between species”: transferred mechanisms could supply components of a rejuvenation intervention. Their origin in a long-lived species would not establish reversal of existing human decline, and LON-02 does not require a cross-species mechanism.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-07, “Control of systemic aging signals through the circulation”: modifying circulating signals could be one route toward coordinated effects across organs. Demonstrating control of such signals would remain distinct from demonstrating durable functional rejuvenation. LON-02 could also require local tissue repair that circulating-signal control alone does not establish.

Disciplinary synthesis: the concept sits within longevity research and overlaps regenerative medicine, gene delivery, oncology, immunology and neuroscience. These fields address complementary requirements: restoring function, reaching target tissues, controlling cancer and immune risks, and preserving brain function. Local eye treatment provides enabling evidence without completing the broader body-wide concept.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not establish the field’s status as of November 2026 or whether subsequent studies materially changed the evidence.
NCT07290244’s study-specific identity, intervention, phase, design, dates and results remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The reason visual-acuity restoration was not observed in 18-month-old mice remains unresolved here; corneal opacity was the authors’ suggested assessment limitation.
Referenced extended data and supplementary materials were absent from the reviewed paper artifact, limiting assessment of details dependent on those materials.
The extent to which a future intervention would correct mutations, cell loss and extracellular damage, or produce immune injury, requires separate evidence.
Clinically meaningful thresholds, follow-up periods, acceptable risks, repeat-treatment schedules and methods for assessing preservation of personal identity remain unspecified proposals.

brief.title: Safe, repeatable recovery from the effects of aging
possible: As you grow older, treatment could restore abilities you have already lost across your organs, including memory and thinking. You could receive treatment again to maintain or renew that recovery while preserving who you are.
why: Established decline from aging could become repairable. For older people, lasting recovery could mean more independence, less disability and less need for care.

sources.who: Yuancheng Lu, Benedikt Brommer, Xiao Tian and colleagues
sources.showed: The researchers changed gene activity in mouse eye cells to restore more youthful cell states. They reported regrowth of damaged nerve fibres and recovery of vision lost through glaucoma, an eye disease, and aging.
sources.quote:
promotes axon
regeneration after injury, and reverses vision loss in a mouse model of glaucoma and
in aged mice.
sources.cited_for: Some lost function in mouse eyes can recover after treatment that resets age-related cell states.
sources.not_established: These experiments do not establish safe, repeatable recovery across an aged human body.

shown: Lu and colleagues reported recovery of reduced visual sharpness and nerve-cell electrical activity in aging mice. Their work demonstrates local recovery in the eye. Visual recovery was not observed in older mice; the researchers suggested that clouded corneas interfered with measurement.
missing: Human studies have yet to demonstrate lasting recovery of established decline across several organs, including memory and thinking.
Treatment must preserve cells’ specialized roles and personal identity, with long-term assessment of cancer, immune injury and other harms.
Repeated treatment must maintain or renew benefits without accumulating harm or losing effectiveness.
Researchers must establish which tissues recover and which damage remains, including mutations, lost cells and damage outside cells.

milestones.label: Lasting recovery across organs, including memory and thinking
milestones.explanation: Randomized, controlled human studies would have to show meaningful, lasting recovery across several organs, including memory and thinking. This would establish restored function beyond younger-looking molecular measurements.

milestones.label: Safety with preserved identity and long-term cancer monitoring
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to assess cells’ specialized roles, immune injury, organ harms, cancer, memory, thinking and personal identity. This would test whether recovery preserves the person and the functions their tissues need.

milestones.label: Repeated treatment sustains benefit without accumulating harm
milestones.explanation: Repeated treatment would have to maintain or renew function while studies track accumulating toxicity, declining effectiveness and delayed harm. This would establish whether recovery can be renewed safely.

milestones.label: Recovery’s reach, duration and remaining damage are defined
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report which tissues and functions recover, how long benefits last and what damage remains. This would define the demonstrated reach of recovery without implying unlimited repetition or survival.

uncertain: The benefit thresholds, acceptable risks and follow-up periods needed to judge success remain unspecified.
How to assess preservation of personal identity remains an open question.
Whether changing cell states can also correct mutations, replace lost cells and repair damage outside cells remains unresolved.

page.title: Repeatable multisystem rejuvenation in humans
page.definition: A treatment restores established age-related loss of function across multiple body systems in older people, including cognition, and maintains or renews recovery after re-treatment. It preserves cognition and personal identity within prospectively defined safety limits.

goal.need: WHO estimated global life expectancy at 73.3 years and healthy life expectancy at 62.8 years in 2023. Their difference is 10.5 years. These population measures describe the gap between survival and health across all causes, providing a quantitative motivation for interventions that recover function.

figures.caption: Global life expectancy and healthy life expectancy in 2023
figures.note: Population estimates covering all causes of impaired health.

statements.quote: their therapeutic treatment restores muscle, cognitive, and immune function by a minimum of 10 years
statements.context: The published minimum functional-restoration objective of XPRIZE Healthspan.

statements.quote: translating epigenetic restoration into a new class of medicines for age-related diseases.
statements.context: Chief Scientific Officer Sharon Rosenzweig-Lipson describes the goal of advancing ER-100 into clinical testing for optic neuropathies.

statements.quote: geroscience and healthspan trials that aim to preserve or improve function
statements.context: Its consensus dated 18 May 2026 discusses clinical endpoints for community-dwelling older adults with early functional decline.

completion.title: A repeat-treatment regimen restores multisystem function and meets prespecified safety and identity tests.
completion.criterion: In a registered controlled study in adults aged 50–90 years, treatment meets the XPRIZE Healthspan 10-year restoration test in muscle, cognition and immunity, and maintains or renews those gains after re-treatment of the same participants. The responder difference is ≥20 percentage points, with a one-sided 90% confidence-interval lower bound ≥15 points. The regimen also meets prespecified endpoints for cognitive and personal-identity preservation, cancer, immune injury and other toxicity over the registered follow-up. The protocol defines the re-treatment interval, follow-up and acceptable risks.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, provisional extension of the XPRIZE Healthspan functional-restoration target to repeat treatment.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA cellular/gene-therapy guidance, XPRIZE Finals rules and the ARPA-H intrinsic-capacity consensus located no repeated whole-body restoration test, long-term safety limits or personal-identity endpoint. The Atlas provisionally uses XPRIZE’s three domains as the minimum multisystem scope and adds re-treatment. Safety, identity and repeat-treatment endpoints still require operational definitions in a registered protocol.

milestones.title: A rejuvenation therapy shows biological activity through its intended delivery route in a preclinical model.
milestones.criterion: For cellular and gene therapies, proof-of-concept studies establish biological activity, feasibility of the intended administration route and a rationale for human testing. Lu and colleagues reported local visual-acuity recovery after four weeks of OCT4, SOX2 and KLF4 expression in mice assessed at 12 months of age. Figure 4b includes 12 treated aged eyes and 14 aged eyes without induced expression. The peer-reviewed paper was published on 2 December 2020.
milestones.set_by: FDA CBER, Frequently Asked Questions—Developing Potential Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, August 2026, question 27. This guidance applies to the cellular/gene-therapy route.
milestones.threshold_quote: POC studies are important to evaluate bioactivity, determine the feasibility of the ROA

milestones.title: A rejuvenation therapy receives authorization for a first-in-human clinical investigation.
milestones.criterion: For the US investigational-drug route, an Investigational New Drug application takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless a clinical hold applies, or earlier upon FDA notification that investigation may begin. Life Biosciences announced FDA clearance of the ER-100 application for optic neuropathies on 28 January 2026. This clearance is documented here through the developer’s announcement.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40(b), governing when an Investigational New Drug application takes effect.
milestones.threshold_quote: On earlier notification by FDA that the clinical investigations in the IND may begin.

milestones.title: A rejuvenation therapy is administered to people in a Phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: An investigational therapy enters human administration under an authorized Phase 1 protocol. Life Biosciences announced the first ER-100 participant’s dosing on 9 June 2026. On 8 October 2026, it reported three participants with open-angle glaucoma receiving 2×10^11 vector genomes into the eye plus doxycycline, with no reported dose-limiting toxicities or serious adverse events through day 56 and a safety-board recommendation for dose escalation. These interim results are a developer press release and are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a), defining Phase 1. The cited human results concern local treatment of optic neuropathies.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A rejuvenation therapy’s human results pass XPRIZE’s clinical proof-of-concept review.
milestones.criterion: XPRIZE judges accept human proof-of-concept findings supporting feasibility, recruitment, dosing and initial safety for advancement to Finals. Teams define their study-specific success criteria. XPRIZE announced 20 Finalist teams on 11 August 2026, including 10 Milestone 2 awardees receiving $1 million each. Selection establishes passage through this review. The cited announcement supplies no participant-level efficacy results.
milestones.set_by: XPRIZE Foundation, Finals Application Guidelines, version 1.0, section on Semi-Finals early-stage and proof-of-concept trials.
milestones.threshold_quote: The Semi-Finals early stage / PoC trials will be evaluated by judges to demonstrate the teams’ feasibility of approach

milestones.title: A treatment restores at least 10 years of function across three systems in a controlled human study.
milestones.criterion: Within one year, a randomized controlled study in adults aged 50–90 demonstrates ≥10-year-equivalent gains across three domains. Responders exceed personalized thresholds in endurance and lower-body power, >50% of selected Cogstate cognitive subtests, and 2 of 3 central immune-biomarker measures. The intention-to-treat intervention–control responder difference is ≥20 percentage points, with a one-sided 90% confidence-interval lower bound ≥15 points. XPRIZE judges assess the results under its Finals rules. Individual response equations and the third immune assay remain unspecified in the located documents.
milestones.set_by: XPRIZE Foundation, Finals Rules and Regulations dated 13 April 2026, sections 8, 11 and 12, supplemented by FAQ Issue 4 dated 8 October 2026.
milestones.threshold_quote: a functional improvement of at least 10 years in all three systems (muscle, cognition, and immune)

not_found: No published completion standard combining multisystem recovery, repeat treatment, long-term safety and preservation of personal identity was located.
The located XPRIZE documents leave individual response equations and the third immune assay pending, and searches did not locate finalized specifications.
No published human result satisfying the XPRIZE three-domain minimum restoration test was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07290244 opened as generic interface text, and its API record could not be retrieved.

results.finding: In aged mice, visual acuity recovered after OSK treatment; 12 treated and 14 uninduced eyes were assessed.
results.detail: OSK was delivered to the eye by AAV and assessed after four weeks; the mice were 12 months old at assessment.
results.quote:
In the absence of OSK induction, there was a significant 
reduction in visual acuity and in RGC electrical activity by 12 months of 
age—a loss that was restored by OSK induction (Fig. 4b, Extended Data 
Fig. 9e).

results.finding: Systemic OSK gene therapy in aged male mice (sample size not stated) extended median remaining lifespan by 109% versus controls.
results.detail: The study used retro-orbital AAV delivery and cyclic induction. It lacked an AAV-only control, included only male mice, and found limited brain OSK expression.
results.quote:
In this study, we show that systemically delivered adeno-associated viruses, encoding an inducible OSK system,
in 124-week-old male mice extend the median remaining lifespan by 109% over WT controls and enhance several
health parameters.

results.finding: Life Biosciences announced FDA clearance of the ER-100 IND on January 28, 2026; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The clearance permits a first-in-human Phase 1 investigation in patients with optic neuropathies.
results.quote: BOSTON, January 28, 2026 – Life Biosciences, Inc., (“Life Bio”) a biotechnology company pioneering cellular rejuvenation therapies to reverse and prevent multiple diseases of aging, today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared its Investigational New Drug (IND) application for ER-100.

results.finding: ER-100 was administered to 3 participants with glaucoma in a Phase 1 trial, with safety observations through day 56.
results.detail: Participants received a single intravitreal dose with daily oral doxycycline. The company reported no dose-limiting toxicities or serious adverse events and a recommendation to escalate the dose.
results.quote: Administration of ER-100 was well-tolerated through Day 56 in three participants with glaucoma, supporting dose escalation in the ongoing trial

results.finding: XPRIZE Healthspan selected 20 finalist teams; participant sample size was not reported.
results.detail: XPRIZE also named 10 Milestone 2 awardees. The announcement reports selection, not participant-level efficacy results.
results.quote: XPRIZE announced 20 Finalist teams today at an awards ceremony in Salt Lake City. Of the Finalists, 10 teams will be awarded $1 million each as Milestone 2 Awardees.
